common_name: TropicSweet Apple (University of Florida Low-Chill Apple)

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter or container trees spring through fall; TropicSweet was developed by the University of Florida for very low chill requirements and benefits from a compatible low-chill pollinator such as Anna or Dorsett Golden nearby.

directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun; TropicSweet is a low-chill apple cultivar developed by the University of Florida specifically for subtropical apple production, requiring roughly 250–300 chill hours — low enough to fruit reliably through most of zone 9 and the warmer parts of zone 8b where standard apple cultivars fail to bloom consistently. It joins Anna, Dorsett Golden, and Ein Shemer as one of the small handful of apples bred or selected specifically for the Deep South and Gulf Coast, and performs best when planted alongside one of those cultivars for cross-pollination, since it is not reliably self-fruitful. Fruit ripens in early to midsummer with a sweet, mild flavor and crisp texture typical of low-chill apple selections, which tend to be less complex in flavor than high-chill Northern apples but offer the major advantage of actually fruiting in a warm-winter climate. Maintain good air circulation through pruning to reduce fire blight and apple scab pressure, both significant disease concerns for apples grown in humid Southern conditions.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Apple Varieties for Florida
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Apple Production in Texas
Petals from the Past Nursery (Alabama) — Low-chill apple variety guide

common_name: Tropic Beauty Apple (Early-Ripening Florida Low-Chill Apple)

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter or container trees spring through fall; Tropic Beauty is a Florida-bred low-chill apple that ripens earlier than most low-chill selections and benefits from a compatible pollinator such as Anna or Dorsett Golden nearby.

directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Tropic Beauty is a Florida-bred low-chill apple cultivar requiring roughly 150–250 chill hours, among the lowest chill requirements of any apple in common cultivation, and is prized in Gulf Coast home orchards for ripening earlier in the season than most other low-chill selections, often just after Dorsett Golden. Fruit is medium-sized with a red blush over a yellow-green background and crisp, mildly sweet-tart flesh — pleasant for fresh eating, though like most low-chill apples the flavor is milder and less complex than high-chill Northern cultivars. Plant with Anna, Dorsett Golden, or Ein Shemer for cross-pollination, since Tropic Beauty is not reliably self-fruitful. Prune annually to an open center to maintain good light penetration and air circulation, which helps limit fire blight and apple scab, the two disease pressures that most commonly trouble apples in the humid Gulf South.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Apple Varieties for Florida
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Apple Production in Texas
Petals from the Past Nursery (Alabama) — Low-chill apple variety guide

common_name: Hyakume Persimmon (Gosho, Nearly Non-Astringent Japanese Persimmon)

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in late winter to early spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Hyakume is self-fruitful, but pollination and seed formation encourage its flesh to develop the brown sugar-flecked pattern that lets it be eaten while still firm.

directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Hyakume, also sold as Gosho, is a large, flattish Japanese kaki persimmon cultivar notable among astringent-type persimmons for a distinctive trait — when the flowers are pollinated and seeds form, the flesh develops streaks and flecks of brown, sugary tissue, and fruit with enough of this coloring can be eaten firm and crisp like a non-astringent type rather than requiring full softening. Unpollinated fruit without seeds remains fully astringent until soft-ripe, so planting near another kaki cultivar for pollination noticeably improves the eating experience. The fruit is large, pale orange, and mild-flavored with a pleasant, slightly spiced sweetness once the brown sugar-flecking develops. Trees are vigorous, productive, and, like most Asian persimmons, largely trouble-free once established, tolerating heat and a range of soils well. Harvest in fall as fruit colors fully; taste-test a fruit or two to judge whether the crop has enough pollination-driven flecking to eat crisp, or whether it needs to soften fully before eating.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Persimmon Production

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring after frost danger has passed; Mexicola Grande is a Type A avocado and sets more fruit with a Type B companion such as Fuerte, Bacon, or Zutano nearby, and shares the exceptional cold-hardiness of its Mexicola parent.

directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun; Mexicola Grande is a larger-fruited selection out of the classic Mexicola avocado line, retaining the same remarkable cold-hardiness that makes Mexican-race avocados the only avocados worth attempting in zone 8b–9, while offering noticeably bigger fruit than the original Mexicola. Like its parent, Mexicola Grande is a pure Mexican-race avocado (Persea americana var. drymifolia) with thin, edible skin carrying a distinctive anise or licorice note, rich, high-oil flesh, and a compact tree form compared to tropical Guatemalan-race cultivars like Hass. Established trees tolerate brief drops into the high teens °F with wood damage but often survive and resprout, whereas standard nursery avocado cultivars are killed outright at those temperatures. Plant with a Type B pollinator such as Fuerte, Bacon, or Zutano for improved fruit set, and harvest in late summer to fall once fruit reaches full size and skin darkens to near-black; slice and eat with the thin skin on for the full anise-inflected flavor.
sources: University of California Cooperative Extension — Cold-Hardy Avocado Varieties
California Avocado Society — Cold Climate Avocado Growing

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring after frost danger has passed in well-drained soil; Duke 7 is a Mexican-race avocado prized for root disease tolerance and cold-hardiness and benefits from a Type B pollinator such as Fuerte nearby for fruit set.

directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun, avoiding low or poorly drained spots; Duke 7 is a Mexican-race avocado selection out of California best known as a Phytophthora root rot-tolerant rootstock, but it is also grown and fruited directly in cold-marginal plantings for the same cold-hardiness that characterizes Mexican-race avocados generally, tolerating brief exposure to around 18°F once well established. Fruit is smaller than commercial Guatemalan or hybrid types like Hass, with thin, often edible skin and rich, high-oil flesh typical of the Mexican race. Because root rot caused by Phytophthora cinnamomi is one of the most serious problems in wet or heavy soils, Duke 7's tolerance is a genuine practical advantage for gardeners without ideal, fast-draining soil — even so, plant on a slight mound or berm and avoid overwatering, since good drainage remains important for avocado health generally. Plant with a Type B pollinator such as Fuerte or Zutano nearby to improve fruit set, and expect a compact, cold-tolerant tree well suited to marginal avocado climates.
sources: University of California Cooperative Extension — Cold-Hardy Avocado Varieties
